sudan.title: من انقلاب 2021 إلى عقوبات 2025.. لماذا ترفض واشنطن استقبال البرهان؟ - العين الإخبارية
sudan.content: من انقلاب 2021 إلى عقوبات 2025.. لماذا ترفض واشنطن استقبال البرهان؟ عاجل الغاء الرئيسية الأخبار آخر الأخبار أخبار مصورة اخترنا لكم سوشيال ميديا الخليج العربي الوطن العربي شؤون دولية سياسة آخر الأخبار التحليلات المغرب العربي شؤون أفريقية الإسلام السياسي اليمن العراق ليبيا اقتصاد أسواق المال عملات رقمية تكنولوجيا سياحة وسفر سيارات الذكاء الاصطناعي الطاقة المتجددة مساحة خضراء الرأي منوعات صحة ثقافة فن شباب علوم وفضاء حوادث بيئة رياضة السعودية الإمارات مصر فيديو إنفوجراف المزيد حوارات العين الإخبارية مراسلو العين الإخبارية تقارير خاصة وثائقيات عينك على العالم إنفوجراف الأحد 2026/11/8 08:59 م وضع ليلي تابعونا على السوشيال ميديا سياسة من انقلاب 2021 إلى عقوبات 2025.. لماذا ترفض واشنطن استقبال البرهان؟ العين الإخبارية الأحد 2026/11/8 12:09 م بتوقيت أبوظبي عبدالفتاح البرهان تم تحديثه الأحد 2026/11/8 02:10 م بتوقيت أبوظبي جددت سلطات بورتسودان انتقادها لواشنطن لرفضها منح قائد الجيش عبدالفتاح البرهان تأشيرة دخول لأراضيها، متجاهلة بذلك دور البرهان في تأجيج حرب السودان. وانتقد ممثل سلطة بورتسودان، عمار محمود، في بيان ألقاه أمام اللجنة السادسة للجمعية العامة للأمم المتحدة، الجمعة، خلال مناقشة البند 165 المتعلق بتقرير لجنة العلاقات مع البلد المضيف، رفض الإدارة الأمريكية إصدار التأشيرة حال دون مشاركة البرهان في اجتماعات الأسبوع رفيع المستوى للجمعية العامة في سبتمبر/أيلول الماضي، معتبراً ذلك إخلالاً باتفاق مقر الأمم المتحدة لعام 1947. إلا أن محمود تجاهل حق واشنطن في منع استخدام أراضيها ومنبر الأمم المتحدة لمنح الشرعية السياسية لقائد عسكري معاقب دولياً، أقام سلطته بالقوة ويواصل من خلالها حرباً مدمرة. ورغم أن سلطة بورتسودان تروج للبرهان في المحافل الدولية باعتباره "رئيس مجلس السيادة الانتقالي"، فإن شرعية هذه الصفة انتهت في 25 أكتوبر/تشرين الأول 2021، عندما انقلب على الوثيقة الدستورية الحاكمة والسلطة المدنية الانتقالية وعطل المؤسسات الشرعية للدولة. وخلال انقلاب جيش البرهان اعتُقل رئيس الوزراء في ذلك الوقت، عبدالله حمدوك وعدد من المسؤولين المدنيين، وجُمّدت مؤسسات الانتقال، وأُعيد القرار السياسي والأمني إلى قيادة الجيش. ومنذ ذلك الحين، لم يحصل البرهان على أي تفويض انتخابي، ولم يقد مساراً انتقالياً يعيد السلطة إلى المدنيين. لا يقوم تبرير واشنطن لرفض التأشيرة على الخلاف السياسي وحده؛ بل أيضا إلى عقوبات فرضتها وزارة الخزانة الأمريكية، في يناير/كانون الثاني 2025، على البرهان بموجب الأمر التنفيذي المتعلق بالأشخاص الذين يزعزعون استقرار السودان ويقوضون هدف الانتقال الديمقراطي. وقالت الخزانة الأمريكية في تبرير فرض العقوبات إن قوات الجيش، تحت قيادة البرهان، نفذت هجمات مميتة على المدنيين، بينها غارات على مدارس وأسواق ومستشفيات، وعرقلت بصورة متكررة ومتعمدة وصول المساعدات، واستخدمت الحرمان من الغذاء وسيلة في الحرب. كما أشارت إلى أن وزير الخارجية الأمريكي خلص، في ديسمبر/كانون الأول 2023، إلى ارتكاب أفراد في الجيش جرائم حرب، واتهمت البرهان باختيار الحرب بدلاً من التفاوض الجاد وخفض التصعيد. وبحسب محللين فإن واشنطن لا تتعامل مع البرهان باعتباره رئيساً محايداً يمثل جميع السودانيين، بل كقائد عسكري مفروض عليه عقوبات تتهمه رسمياً بتهديد السلام والاستقرار، وتقويض الانتقال المدني، وارتبط اسمه بهجمات على المدنيين والأعيان المحمية. كما أن الرفض الأمريكي يستند إلى منطق سياسي وحقوقي واضح؛ إذ لا ينبغي أن تتحول الجمعية العامة إلى منصة لتطبيع سلطة قائد انقلابي أو تبييض سجل الحرب والانتهاكات بخطاب دبلوماسي، في وقت تواصل فيه قواته القتال وتواجه اتهامات بارتكاب فظائع ضد المدنيين واستخدام أسلحة كيميائية محرمة دولياً، بينما تتمسك قيادته بخيار الحسم العسكري وترفض وقف الحرب أو قبول هدنة إنسانية، بحسب محللين. كما أن القانون الأمريكي يتمسك بحق الولايات المتحدة في حماية أمنها والسيطرة على دخول الأجانب الذين تعدّهم تهديداً لأمنها إلى أراضيها خارج منطقة مقر الأمم المتحدة ومحيطها الضروري. وتمثل هذه الاعتبارات النافذة القانونية الأقوى التي يمكن أن تستند إليها واشنطن، شريطة وجود تقييم أمني محدد، وعدم استخدام الاستثناء على نحو يلغي التزاماتها بموجب اتفاق المقر. السودان غرفة الأخبار #شؤون_سودانية #شؤون_أمريكية أخبار ذات صلة متحدث «منسقية النازحين» بالسودان يحذر من وضع لا يحتمل الانتظار (خاص) اقرأ الخبر «كيماوي السودان».. أدلة تتراكم ومساءلة دولية غائبة (خاص) اقرأ الخبر عقوبات أسترالية على طرفي حرب السودان.. وكتيبة إخوانية في القائمة اقرأ الخبر غارات الجيش السوداني على الأسواق.. «صدمة» أممية ومطالب بوقف الهجمات اقرأ الخبر عاجل العين الإخبارية منذ 21 ساعة الرئيس الإسرائيلي إسحق هرتسوغ يبلغ غادي آيزنكوت بتكليفه بتشكيل الحكومة الجديدة منذ 21 ساعة الرئيس الإسرائيلي إسحق هرتسوغ يبلغ غادي آيزنكوت بتكليفه بتشكيل الحكومة الجديدة منذ 1 يوم جرحى بإطلاق نار في ثاني كبرى مدن بولندا واعتقال منفذه منذ 2 يوم سماع دوي انفجارين في محيط منطقة سوزا في جزيرة قشم الإيرانية ولا أنباء عن إصابات تريند فن «قطعة علكة».. تصرف عفوي لمارت رمضان ديمير يفاجئ الصحفيين فن محمد الحلو يغادر المستشفى ويطمئن جمهوره على حالته الصحية منوعات قرار نهائي كاريكاتير فن حظك اليوم تليفزيون ثقافة مرأة و منوعات صحة ألبومات مقالات تكنولوجيا محافظات فيديو 7 محمد الشناوي يقترب من العودة لقائمة منتخب مصر استعداداً لملاوي السيدة انتصار السيسى تنعى ضحايا قطاري العياط وتوجه الهلال الأحمر بتقديم الدعم النيابة العامة تباشر التحقيقات فى حادث تصادم قطارين بالعياط وتشكل لجنة فنية الصحة: ارتفاع مصابى حادث قطارى العياط لـ112 مصابًا و7 وفيات.. وخروج 45 حالة وزارة الثقافة تُهدي مدرسة بطلة تحدى القراءة بالعربي 3000 كتاب ومجلة النيابة الإدارية تطلق منصتها القضائية الرقمية لتطوير منظومة العدالة طرابزون يتقدم على ألانيا سبور بثنائية فى الشوط الأول وصلاح يسجل.. فيديو علي ماهر يعلن تشكيل الجهاز المعاون لمنتخب مصر محمد صلاح يسجل هدف طرابزون سبور الثاني ضد ألانيا.. فيديو من أصول مغربية.. من هو غادي آيزنكوت رئيس حكومة الاحتلال الإسرائيلي الجديد الرئيسية تحقيقات وملفات السودان بين الحرب والجوع مع أكبر أزمة نزوح عالمية.. مفوضية اللاجئين: 15.4 مليون شخص يبحثون عن مأوى آمن وسط صراع لا يتوقف.. والأمم المتحدة تحذر من تفاقم الأزمة ووقف المساعدات عن 90% من المحتاجين الأحد، 08 نوفمبر 2026 03:00 ص السودان فيسبوك واتساب كتبت: هند المغربي أكثر من ثلاث سنوات من الحرب كفيلة بتحويل حياة ملايين السودانيين إلى رحلة مستمرة من النزوح والفقدان، بعدما أجبرتهم المعارك المتصاعدة على ترك منازلهم بحثًا عن الأمان، ليواجهوا واقعًا أكثر قسوة في مخيمات النزوح ومناطق العودة، حيث تتراجع المساعدات الإنسانية وتتزايد الاحتياجات، بينما تقف المنظمات الأممية عاجزة عن تلبية أبسط متطلبات الحياة من مأوى وغذاء وحماية. من جانبها حذرت الأمم المتحدة من أن النزاع في السودان يواصل تعميق معاناة المدنيين بعد مرور ثلاث سنوات ونصف على اندلاعه، حيث تجبر التحولات في خطوط المواجهة المزيد من العائلات على الفرار، مما يترك الكثيرين منهم بلا مأوى في ظل نقص حاد في التمويل. السودان يوصف بأنه أكبر ازمة نزوح في العالم مفوضية الأمم المتحدة لشؤون اللاجئين أكدت أن نحو 15.4 مليون شخص بحاجة ماسة إلى مأوى طارئ ومستلزمات منزلية أساسية، بمن فيهم ملايين الأشخاص الذين قرروا العودة إلى مناطقهم الأصلية، ومع ذلك، لا تستطيع الوكالات الإنسانية تقديم المساعدة سوى لنحو 10% فقط من المحتاجين بسبب قيود التمويل، مما يخلق فجوة كبيرة بين الاحتياجات المتزايدة والموارد المتاحة للاستجابة لها. ووفق الهجرة الدولية أنه على الرغم من أن السودان يواجه أكبر أزمة نزوح في العالم، إلا أن خطة الاحتياجات والاستجابة الإنسانية لعام 2026 تعاني من نقص حاد في التمويل، حيث لم تحصل الخطة سوى على 47% من المبلغ مما دفع هذا الوضع الوكالات الإنسانية إلى تقليص الخدمات الأساسية بشكل أكبر، علما بأن الخطط الأصلية كانت تهدف إلى دعم 20.4 مليون شخص فقط من أصل 33.7 مليون محتاج في جميع أنحاء البلاد. معاناة العائلات السودانية من جانبه أشار أبو بكر جالو، نائب ممثل مفوضية الأمم المتحدة لشؤون اللاجئين في السودان إلى أن ثلاثة من كل أربعة نازحين في البلاد هم من النساء والأطفال موضحا بالنسبة لامرأة فقدت كل شيء، لا يقتصر معنى الخيمة على كونها مجرد مأوى، فهي تمثل الفرق بين النوم في العراء محاطة بأشخاص غرباء، وبين الحصول على مساحة خاصة بها. إنها تعني الكرامة والخصوصية والأمان لتلك المرأة وعائلتها". وأشار جالو إلى أن ظاهرة الـنينيو تسببت في هطول أمطار أقل بكثير من المعدل الطبيعي في السودان هذا العام، مما أثر على الحصاد في دارفور وكردفان ومناطق أخرى متضررة بالفعل من القتال المستمر. ولفت إلى أنه في مثل هذا الوقت من العام، عادة ما تكون أسعار الغذاء ميسورة التكلفة أكثر نظرا لانتهاء موسم الحصاد، لكن الأسعار لا تزال مرتفعة بشكل مؤلم مؤكدا بالنسبة لعائلة فقدت كل ما تملك، فإن كل جنيه سوداني ينفق على الغذاء يعني مالا لا يمكن إنفاقه على شراء بطانية أو مستلزمات لتوفير مأوى آمن. مستودعات المنظمات الإنسانية فارغة وقال محمد رفعت، رئيس بعثة المنظمة الدولية للهجرة في السودان إن مستودعات المنظمة باتت فارغة تماما الآن مشير الي أن 16 شاحنة تمكنت يوم أمس من الوصول إلى دارفور، لكنها كانت آخر ما لدي المنظمة من مخزون في مستودعاتها وأكد رفعت أن في حين عاد أكثر من 5.2 مليون شخص إلى مناطقهم الأصلية،لا يعودون بالضرورة إلى منازلهم، إذ تعرض الكثير منها للتدمير أو النهب. وأشار إلى أنه مع استمرار غياب الرعاية الصحية والكهرباء والمياه في مناطق عودتهم، قد يضطر هؤلاء الأشخاص إلى المغادرة مجددا، دون أي أمل في العودة مرة أخرى. الامم المتحدة السودان الهجرة الدولية مفوضية اللاجئين تابعوا آخر أخبار اليوم السابع عبر Google News اشترك في قناة sudan.summary: تواجه السودان أكبر أزمة نزوح في العالم، حيث يقدر عدد النازحين بـ 15.4 مليون شخص يبحثون عن مأوى آمن وسط صراع مستمر منذ ثلاث سنوات ونصف. وفقًا لمفوضية الأمم المتحدة لشؤون اللاجئين، فإن 90% من المحتاجين لا يتلقون المساعدات اللازمة، مما يزيد من معاناتهم. تتراجع المساعدات الإنسانية بشكل كبير، حيث لم يتمكن التمويل من تغطية سوى 10% من الاحتياجات الأساسية، مما يترك الفجوة بين الطلب والموارد متسعة. يعاني النازحون، ومعظمهم من النساء والأطفال، من نقص حاد في الغذاء والمأوى، حيث ارتفعت أسعار المواد الغذائية بشكل مؤلم. كما أن الظروف المناخية السيئة أثرت على المحاصيل، مما زاد من تفاقم الوضع. في ظل هذه الظروف، تواجه العائلات صعوبة في العودة إلى مناطقهم الأصلية، حيث تفتقر هذه المناطق إلى الخدمات الأساسية مثل الرعاية الصحية والمياه.

ethiopia.title: How Ethiopia’s Military Modernization Is Emerging as Strategic Pillar of Regional Stability” - ENA English
ethiopia.content: How Ethiopia’s Military Modernization Is Emerging as Strategic Pillar of Regional Stability? - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content How Ethiopia’s Military Modernization Is Emerging as Strategic Pillar of Regional Stability? - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us How Ethiopia’s Military Modernization Is Emerging as Strategic Pillar of Regional Stability? 🔇Unmute By Staff Writer November 8 , 2026 (ENA) Ethiopia’s growing military and technological capabilities are becoming increasingly significant, not only for safeguarding its national security but also for advancing peace, stability and economic integration in the Horn of Africa. By modernising its defence institutions, strengthening its air force and investing in advanced military technology, the country has enhanced its capacity to address emerging security challenges while contributing to a more secure and stable regional environment. The current acquisition of 12 fighter jets from Russia marks another step in Ethiopia’s efforts to modernise its military capabilities. Beyond strengthening national defence, such technological advancements can contribute to regional security by enhancing the country's capacity to deter threats, respond to security emergencies and support collective efforts to maintain peace. Rather than viewing military modernisation exclusively through the lens of geopolitical competition, greater attention should be given to its broader contribution to regional stability, security cooperation and economic integration. In this regard, Ethiopia’s defence modernisation offers significant benefits that extend beyond safeguarding its national sovereignty and territorial integrity. Its advancing military technology and growing operational capabilities can strengthen regional security, enhance collective responses to shared security challenges, deter potential threats and contribute to a more stable environment. Through responsible military development, Ethiopia can also help build trust among regional partners by demonstrating that strong defence institutions and peaceful cooperation are complementary objectives. In particular, advancements in air power can improve the country's capacity to protect its airspace, support regional security cooperation and respond to emerging threats. These capabilities can further contribute to protecting strategic infrastructure, securing cross-border trade routes and creating favourable conditions for regional economic cooperation and integration. A technologically advanced and professionally organised defence force is an important component of both national and regional security. In a region facing terrorism, cross-border criminal activities, political instability and other transnational threats, the ability of states to protect their territories and respond effectively to emerging challenges is essential. Ethiopia's investment in defence technology, particularly in air power, surveillance capabilities and operational readiness, therefore, can strengthen its ability to address security threats that extend beyond national borders. Modern military systems can improve situational awareness, enhance the protection of critical infrastructure and facilitate timely responses to security emergencies. Stronger defence capabilities also contribute to deterrence, reducing the likelihood of potential adversaries resorting to military confrontation. When supported by responsible defence policies, transparency and diplomatic engagement, military preparedness can reinforce confidence in national security institutions and contribute to a more predictable regional security environment. Hence, Ethiopia's military modernisation should be viewed as part of the broader effort to build the institutional and technological capacity required to safeguard peace and stability in the Horn of Africa. The security challenges confronting the Horn of Africa are interconnected and cannot be effectively addressed by individual countries acting alone. They require coordinated responses and stronger regional security partnerships. Ethiopia's growing military capabilities can enhance its contribution to these collective efforts by strengthening its capacity to participate in regional peace and security initiatives as advanced defence technology can improve operational preparedness, intelligence assessment, border protection and the ability to respond to emerging threats. Ethiopia has a longstanding role in regional peace and security efforts, including its engagement in African and international peacekeeping initiatives. Its experience and institutional capabilities provide an important foundation for continued cooperation with neighbouring countries and regional organisations. Peace and security are fundamental prerequisites for sustainable economic integration. Regional trade, cross-border investment, transport networks, energy cooperation and infrastructure development all depend on a stable and predictable security environment. The Horn of Africa possesses considerable economic potential because of its strategic geographical position, natural resources, expanding markets and opportunities for regional connectivity. However, persistent insecurity can undermine investment, disrupt trade routes, damage infrastructure and discourage economic cooperation. Ethiopia's strong defence capabilities helps address these challenges by improving the protection of strategic infrastructure, transportation corridors and economic assets. A capable defence institution can also help create the security conditions necessary for implementing regional development projects. This is particularly important as countries in the region pursue greater economic connectivity through road networks, railway systems, energy interconnections, ports and trade corridors. Protecting these shared economic interests requires not only diplomatic cooperation but also adequate national and regional security capabilities. Consequently, advances in military technology also have an economic dimension when they contribute to protecting the foundations of regional development and integration. The development of air power is another important element of modern defence systems, particularly in geographically extensive regions where security threats can emerge across difficult terrain and national borders. Ethiopia's modernisation of its air force can strengthen its capacity to monitor its airspace, protect national infrastructure and respond to emergencies. Modern aircraft and associated technological systems can also improve operational coordination and support humanitarian and disaster-response activities where appropriate. The broader regional value of these capabilities lies in their potential contribution to security cooperation. Through appropriate bilateral and multilateral arrangements, countries can strengthen information sharing, coordinate responses to common threats and establish mechanisms for preventing security incidents. Such cooperation can help ensure that advances in military technology become instruments of collective security rather than sources of mistrust. It also highlights the importance of combining military preparedness with diplomatic engagement and confidence-building measures. Ethiopia's defence development should therefore be understood within the context of its legitimate national security interests and its broader responsibility to contribute to a peaceful neighbourhood. In this context, narratives portray Ethiopia's defence advancements, including some media coverage emerging from Egypt, as inherently threatening risk diverting attention from the broader importance of regional security cooperation. Such interpretations can deepen mistrust and complicate diplomatic relations. Countries in the region would benefit more from constructive engagement, mutual respect and dialogue than from interpreting one another's national defence developments as grounds for confrontation. The relationship between defence capabilities and economic development is particularly important in a region where insecurity can undermine major development ambitions. Strong institutions, secure borders and protected infrastructure provide an enabling environment for trade, investment and regional connectivity. Ethiopia's military and technological development can also contribute to these objectives by strengthening national resilience and supporting the security requirements of regional cooperation. In conclusion, Ethiopia's advancing military technology represents an important development with implications extending beyond national defence. Its potential contribution to regional peace, stability and economic integration lies in strengthening the capacity to deter security threats, support collective security initiatives and protect the infrastructure and economic corridors upon which regional cooperation depends. The Horn of Africa needs a security environment that enables countries to expand trade, connect markets, develop shared infrastructure and pursue common economic interests. Achieving this requires capable national institutions, stronger regional partnerships and a shared commitment to resolving differences peacefully. Ethiopia's military modernisation should therefore be assessed within this broader regional context. The objective should not be to turn technological advancement into a source of rivalry, but to ensure that stronger defence capabilities contribute to a more secure neighbourhood and a more integrated region. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden
ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia's military modernization is increasingly seen as a strategic pillar for regional stability in the Horn of Africa. By enhancing its defense capabilities, including the acquisition of advanced military technology such as fighter jets from Russia, Ethiopia aims to bolster national security while contributing to regional peace and economic integration. The modernization efforts focus on improving air power, surveillance, and operational readiness, which are essential for addressing security threats that transcend national borders. Ethiopia's advancements can facilitate better responses to emergencies, protect critical infrastructure, and support regional security cooperation. Furthermore, a strong military presence can deter potential adversaries and create a stable environment conducive to economic development. The article emphasizes that Ethiopia's military developments should be viewed as part of a broader effort to foster regional cooperation and security, rather than as a source of geopolitical tension. Ultimately, a secure Horn of Africa is vital for sustainable economic growth and integration among neighboring countries. (160 words)

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Links Nile Water Talks to Egypt’s Support for Red Sea Access - https://kulu-media.com/
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Nile Talks Linked to Red Sea Access Demand | Kulu Media Home Latest News Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea Sudan Africa World Politics Economy Finance Business Education More Analysis Entertainment Tech Health Sports English English ትግርኛ አማርኛ Connect with us Search Kulu Media Ethiopia Links Nile Water Talks to Egypt’s Support for Red Sea Access Home Latest News Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea Sudan Africa World Politics Economy Finance Business Education More Analysis Entertainment Tech Health Sports English English ትግርኛ አማርኛ Home » News » Ethiopia » Ethiopia Links Nile Water Talks to Egypt’s Support for Red Sea Access Ethiopia Ethiopia Links Nile Water Talks to Egypt’s Support for Red Sea Access Ethiopian minister connects Nile negotiations with maritime access ambitions. Published 26 minutes ago on November 8, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk An aerial view of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on Ethiopia's Blue Nile River. Ethiopia's water minister has linked prospects for understanding with Egypt over Nile water management to support for Ethiopia's Red Sea access ambitions. Photo: GERD Ethiopia has raised the prospect of linking negotiations over Nile River water management to Egypt’s support for its pursuit of Red Sea access, introducing another contentious issue into an already strained diplomatic relationship between Addis Ababa and Cairo. Ethiopian Minister of Water and Energy Habtamu Itefa said Egypt should help Ethiopia secure access to the sea, suggesting that such cooperation could create an opportunity for understanding over the Nile dispute. Speaking in an interview broadcast by Al Arabiya , Habtamu presented Ethiopia’s maritime ambitions and Nile water development as strategic interests that Egypt should recognize. The remarks, reported on November 5, represent a significant expansion of Ethiopia’s diplomatic argument, connecting two issues that have increasingly shaped political and security relations across the Horn of Africa. Egypt, however, has maintained that negotiations over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) should focus on a legally binding framework protecting the water security of downstream countries. The disagreement comes amid growing regional tensions involving Ethiopia, Egypt, Eritrea and Sudan, whose leaders have taken increasingly divergent positions on Nile water management and Red Sea governance. In October, Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia adopted an Alamein joint declaration reaffirming their positions on regional sovereignty, Nile water security and responsibility for governing the Red Sea. Habtamu’s latest remarks suggest that Addis Ababa is seeking greater recognition of its maritime interests alongside its right to develop water resources originating within Ethiopian territory. In a separate interview with Fana Media Corporation , the minister criticized Egypt’s approach to Nile water negotiations and argued that Ethiopia’s environmental and infrastructure investments benefit downstream countries. He said Ethiopia had planted more than 56 billion trees over the past seven to eight years, including in the Abbay, Tekeze and Baro river basins, contributing to watershed conservation and water availability. Habtamu argued that Egypt should acknowledge those efforts rather than accuse Ethiopia of threatening its water security. The minister also criticized Egypt’s cultivation of water-intensive crops, particularly rice and sugarcane, saying Cairo should reconsider its own water consumption practices. Those claims reflect Ethiopia’s position in the dispute and do not establish that Egypt’s water shortages are primarily caused by agricultural practices. Habtamu maintained that Ethiopia does not intend to prevent Nile waters from reaching downstream countries, while insisting that the country will continue developing its rivers for electricity generation, irrigation and economic growth. He also rejected the idea that Ethiopia requires approval from Egypt or any other country to construct dams within its sovereign territory. In another Fana interview , Habtamu described the GERD as a symbol of national sovereignty and said Ethiopia would continue pursuing additional water infrastructure projects. The GERD, built on the Blue Nile near Ethiopia’s border with Sudan, remains central to the dispute. Ethiopia considers the project essential for expanding electricity generation and supporting national development, while Egypt and Sudan have repeatedly sought enforceable arrangements governing its operation. The latest disagreement follows a joint meeting of Egyptian and Sudanese foreign and irrigation ministers in Cairo on November 2. In their official joint declaration , the two governments reaffirmed their opposition to what they described as unilateral Ethiopian actions in the Eastern Nile Basin. They argued that the absence of a binding legal framework for operating the GERD creates continuing risks for downstream water security. Egypt and Sudan also emphasized their existing water allocations under the 1959 Nile Waters Agreement and called for renewed cooperation based on prior notification, consultation and the prevention of significant harm. Ethiopia is not a party to the 1959 agreement between Egypt and Sudan and has long rejected the argument that historical allocations can restrict its own development rights. The countries also remain divided over the Nile Basin Cooperative Framework Agreement, which Ethiopia supports as a mechanism for more inclusive management of the river’s resources. Egypt and Sudan have not joined that framework and continue to seek arrangements addressing their concerns about existing water uses and future development projects. The Cairo declaration also addressed the Red Sea, asserting that responsibility for its governance belongs to countries bordering the waterway. Egypt and Sudan opposed maritime arrangements for landlocked countries that would undermine the sovereignty, territorial integrity or security of coastal states. Their position does not amount to a rejection of every form of commercial port access for landlocked countries, but it places clear conditions on how such access should be negotiated. Ethiopia, which has been landlocked since Eritrea’s independence in 1993, has repeatedly identified reliable maritime access as a national economic and strategic priority. The issue has already complicated its relationships with several neighboring governments. Ethiopia’s January 2024 memorandum of understanding with Somaliland generated strong objections from Somalia, which regards Somaliland as part of its sovereign territory. The dispute was subsequently addressed through Turkish-mediated negotiations and the December 2024 Ankara Declaration. Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has since said his government is prepared to discuss Ethiopian sea access through arrangements that respect Somalia’s sovereignty and internationally accepted procedures. Meanwhile, Ethiopia’s pursuit of maritime access has become a major issue in its deteriorating relations with Eritrea. Ethiopian officials have continued calling for regional cooperation on maritime security, including proposals for collective Red Sea security , while tensions between Addis Ababa and Asmara remain high. The broader diplomatic confrontation has also been accompanied by security allegations. In October, Ethiopia’s military chief accused Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan of supporting TPLF-aligned forces, allegations that have not been independently substantiated. These tensions provide the backdrop to Habtamu’s latest remarks, although no agreement has been announced linking Egyptian support for Ethiopia’s maritime ambitions to a settlement over Nile water management. Cairo has previously rejected reports suggesting that it would trade concessions over the GERD for Ethiopian access to the Red Sea. The latest statements therefore highlight a widening diplomatic disagreement rather than a negotiated arrangement. With Ethiopia continuing to defend its right to develop the Nile and Egypt and Sudan demanding binding protections for downstream water security, the prospect of renewed negotiations remains uncertain. Habtamu’s proposal adds another issue to those talks, raising the question of whether the countries can address their competing water and maritime interests through separate negotiations or a broader regional diplomatic process. Published 4 days ago on November 4, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed (left) and Sudanese military leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan (right), pictured in a composite image as diplomatic tensions between the two countries escalate. Image: Kulu Media (Illustration) Ethiopia has ordered six Sudanese consular staff members to leave the country within 48 hours, deepening a diplomatic dispute between the neighboring countries amid allegations involving Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia. A senior Ethiopian official confirmed the departure order to Reuters in a report published on November 4, 2026. The six officials were stationed at Sudan’s consulate in Assosa, the capital of Ethiopia’s Benishangul-Gumuz region near the Sudanese border. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, did not explain the reason for the decision. Ethiopia’s government had not publicly provided a detailed explanation of the move at the time of the Reuters report. The expulsion order comes amid worsening relations between Addis Ababa and Khartoum, with both governments accusing each other of involvement in armed conflicts affecting the wider Horn of Africa. Sudan has accused Ethiopia of allowing the RSF to use Ethiopian territory to launch drone attacks against civilian infrastructure inside Sudan. Khartoum says it has submitted complaints to the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council over the alleged attacks. The latest accusations follow months of Ethiopia-Sudan tensions involving border security, drone operations and the wider Sudanese civil war. Sudanese military officials have previously alleged that RSF drones were being launched from Ethiopian territory, claims rejected by Addis Ababa. Ethiopia denies supporting the RSF. The allegations concerning the use of Ethiopian territory for drone operations have not been independently established. The diplomatic dispute has intensified as Sudan’s civil war continues and renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia raises concerns about the security of the region’s shared borders. Ethiopia, meanwhile, has accused neighboring countries of supporting TPLF-aligned forces involved in renewed hostilities against the Ethiopian federal government. The accusations specifically concern Sudan, Eritrea and Egypt, all of which have denied supporting the armed groups. The competing allegations have heightened tensions between governments already facing significant security and diplomatic challenges. Assosa’s location gives the latest development particular significance. The town lies in western Ethiopia, close to Sudan, and serves as an important administrative center in a region affected by cross-border security concerns. Sudan’s consular presence there has provided a channel for official communication and assistance to Sudanese nationals. The departure of the six staff members could further complicate diplomatic engagement, although the immediate consequences for consular services remain unclear. The latest development follows a series of diplomatic confrontations involving Ethiopia and neighboring countries. On October 1, Ethiopia ordered the closure of its embassy in Eritrea and expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats, accusing Asmara of activities threatening Ethiopian national security. Eritrea subsequently announced that it was severing diplomatic relations with Ethiopia, while the two governments exchanged accusations over the renewed conflict in northern Ethiopia. The deterioration in relations coincided with reports of Eritrean military movements inside eastern Tigray and drone strikes reportedly targeting Eritrean forces. The reported incidents further increased concerns about a wider regional confrontation. The diplomatic dispute also extended to Egypt after Addis Ababa ordered an Egyptian diplomat to leave the country and Cairo responded with a reciprocal measure. The African Union called for restraint and urged the governments involved to resolve their differences through diplomatic channels. The growing tensions have renewed concerns that separate conflicts in Ethiopia and Sudan could become increasingly interconnected. Sudan’s civil war began in April 2023 following a power struggle between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the RSF. The conflict has caused widespread destruction, mass displacement and one of the world’s most severe humanitarian emergencies. According to Reuters, more than 14 million people have been displaced by the fighting. The war has also complicated relations with Sudan’s neighbors, particularly as rival parties accuse regional governments of providing military assistance or allowing armed groups to operate across borders. The regional security implications have become increasingly serious as Sudan’s conflict intersects with diplomatic rivalries involving Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt. Military movements near the Ethiopia-Sudan border and competing allegations of foreign support have added to concerns about wider instability. Eritrea has also accused Ethiopia of supporting Sudan’s RSF and destabilizing the Horn of Africa. Addis Ababa has denied supporting the paramilitary group, and the allegations have not been independently verified. In Ethiopia, the renewed confrontation involving federal forces and TPLF-aligned forces has raised fresh concerns about the durability of the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement, which ended the major phase of the earlier Tigray war. The security situation in northern Ethiopia remains fragile. In October, reported drone strikes near Adigrat were followed by accounts of Eritrean troop movements, illustrating how the renewed conflict has affected relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Sudanese presidential adviser Amjad Farid said Khartoum was seeking to avoid an open war with Ethiopia despite the worsening diplomatic situation. Speaking to Reuters, Farid said Sudan remained committed to defending its territory while making efforts to prevent a direct military confrontation. The departure order for the six Sudanese consular staff members adds another layer of uncertainty to relations between Addis Ababa and Khartoum. It remains unclear whether the measure will lead to further diplomatic restrictions, reciprocal expulsions or renewed negotiations between the two governments. With Sudan’s civil war continuing and security tensions rising across northern and western Ethiopia, the latest dispute underscores the risk that unresolved regional disagreements could further undermine stability across the Horn of Africa. Continue Reading World Ethiopian-American Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia During Tigray War Period US contractor admits passing classified intelligence to Ethiopian officials during conflict. Published 4 days ago on November 4, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk The US Department of Justice headquarters in Washington, D.C. The department announced that Abraham Teklu Lemma pleaded guilty to transmitting classified intelligence to Ethiopian officials. Credit: APK / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 4.0 An Ethiopian-born American citizen who previously worked as a US government contractor has pleaded guilty to providing highly classified American intelligence to Ethiopian officials during a period that overlapped with the Tigray war, according to the US Department of Justice. Abraham Teklu Lemma, a Maryland resident who held a Top Secret security clearance, admitted on November 3, 2026, to conspiring to transmit US national defense information to the Ethiopian government. Prosecutors said the intelligence concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia and was supplied to senior officials within the country’s political, military and intelligence institutions. In an official announcement , the Justice Department said Lemma worked as an information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the US Department of State and the Department of Justice. According to court documents, Lemma collected and transmitted dozens of highly classified documents, notes, photographs and other materials between 2021 and his arrest in August 2023. Some of the information carried the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information classification, one of the highest levels of protection applied to US national security intelligence. Prosecutors said Lemma used his access as an IT administrator to retrieve classified information from government systems. He also copied sensitive information into handwritten notes and secretly carried them outside secure facilities. The Justice Department said these activities enabled him to pass restricted intelligence to Ethiopian government officials over an extended period. The case has drawn particular attention because the alleged espionage activities coincided with Ethiopia’s devastating northern conflict, which began in November 2020 and involved federal forces, TPLF-aligned forces and other armed actors. Although US authorities did not explicitly identify the conflict as the Tigray war in their November 3 announcement, the period covered by Lemma’s activities substantially overlaps with the fighting and its aftermath. The AFP report published on November 4 also noted the connection between the timeline of the intelligence disclosures and the conflict involving Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). US prosecutors said Lemma went beyond transmitting intelligence and, on some occasions, encouraged Ethiopian officials to take direct military action against armed groups opposing the federal government. In one exchange dated December 18, 2021, Lemma reportedly told an Ethiopian official that the opposing fighters had to be defeated to achieve peace. Later that day, according to the Justice Department, he transmitted additional information and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].” The reference to drones is particularly significant because unmanned aircraft were used during Ethiopia’s northern conflict. However, the department did not identify a specific drone operation resulting from that communication or publicly establish that a particular attack was carried out because of Lemma’s message. US officials also said the intelligence he provided was used in military operations. Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, stated that Ethiopian officials used classified national defense information supplied by Lemma during the conflict. Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said Lemma had exploited his privileged access to remove sensitive information from secure facilities and transmit it to Ethiopian officials in the hope that it would help them target and kill opposing fighters. The department’s statements establish the US government’s account of the espionage and its military implications, but they do not publicly identify specific individuals killed, military targets attacked or operations directly
ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia's Water Minister, Habtamu Itefa, has linked negotiations over Nile water management to Egypt's support for Ethiopia's access to the Red Sea, complicating an already tense diplomatic relationship. In a recent interview, he suggested that cooperation on maritime access could foster understanding regarding the Nile dispute. Ethiopia's ambitions for Red Sea access are seen as strategic, especially since it has been landlocked since Eritrea's independence in 1993. Habtamu criticized Egypt's approach to Nile negotiations, arguing that Ethiopia's environmental efforts benefit downstream countries and that Egypt should reconsider its own water-intensive agricultural practices. Meanwhile, Egypt and Sudan have emphasized the need for a legally binding framework to protect their water security, rejecting unilateral Ethiopian actions. The ongoing disagreements highlight the complexities of regional diplomacy, as both nations struggle to reconcile their competing interests over water and maritime access, with no clear resolution in sight. The situation remains precarious amid rising tensions in the Horn of Africa.

Read Ethiopia ranks 30th in Governance Index as security decline offsets gains By our staff reporter, Photo by Anteneh Aklilu November 8, 2026 Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp Ethiopia ranks joint 30th among Africa’s 54 countries in the 2026 Ibrahim Index of African Governance, with improvements in economic opportunity and human development partly offset by a deterioration in security and the rule of law. The country scored 48.4 out of 100 for Overall Governance in 2025, below the continental average of 50.1 but above the East African average of 47.5. Its overall score improved by 1.8 points between 2016 and 2025, according to the Mo Ibrahim Foundation’s country profile. Despite that decade-long improvement, the foundation placed Ethiopia in its “Warning Signs” trend category. Ethiopia shares 30th place with Zimbabwe, which follows a different trajectory classified as “Increasing Improvement”. Released on October 31, the 2026 index assesses governance performance over the decade from 2016 to 2025 across four categories: Security & Rule of Law; Participation, Rights & Inclusion; Foundations for Economic Opportunity; and Human Development. Foundations for Economic Opportunity was Ethiopia’s strongest-performing category, scoring 54.5 out of 100 in 2025 after gaining 4.8 points over the decade. Human Development scored 53.6, an improvement of 1.8 points. Participation, Rights & Inclusion also improved over the full period, rising by 2.7 points to 41.5. It nevertheless remained Ethiopia’s lowest-scoring category. Security & Rule of Law moved in the opposite direction, falling by 2.4 points to 43.8. The decline constrained the country’s overall progress, illustrating the uneven performance behind its aggregate score. The findings distinguish between Ethiopia’s position in 2025 and its progress over the preceding decade: the country recorded a net improvement in Overall Governance, but its score remained below the African average and its trend carried the foundation’s warning classification. Within East Africa, Ethiopia ranked below Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania and Uganda, which placed 10th, 14th, 18th and 28th respectively. It ranked above Djibouti in 35th place, Eritrea in 51st, Sudan in 52nd, Somalia in 53rd and South Sudan in 54th. The rankings also show that a country’s current position does not necessarily reflect the direction of its governance performance. South Sudan, despite ranking last, was classified as showing “Increasing Improvement”, while fifth-ranked South Africa was classified as experiencing “Increasing Deterioration”. Across Africa, the foundation reported slight improvement in Overall Governance over the decade, driven primarily by economic opportunity and human development. Foundations for Economic Opportunity improved in 44 countries, home to 68 per cent of the continent’s population. Infrastructure recorded the largest improvement among the index’s 16 subcategories, advancing in 52 countries—all except Nigeria and Gambia. The gains were led by mobile connectivity and improved access to energy and the internet. However, Security & Rule of Law deteriorated in 34 countries, while Participation, Rights & Inclusion declined in 31 countries. These countries account for 78 per cent and 60 per cent of Africa’s population respectively. Mo Ibrahim, the foundation’s founder and chair, warned that economic and social progress could not sustainably substitute for stronger institutions and security. “Economic and social gains will not last, and will anyway always be weaker, without progress in security, rule of law and participation,” he said. The index draws on 96 indicators using data from 51 African and international sources. The foundation cautions against comparing results directly across different editions because its datasets are continually updated; historical changes should instead be assessed within the same edition. ethiopia.content: UK warns citizens against non-essential travel to Moyale amid Ethiopia clashes - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY UK warns citizens against non-essential travel to Moyale amid Ethiopia clashes Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ by FELIX KIPKEMOI Saturday November 7, 2026 British Embassy in Nairobi/FILE The United Kingdom has cautioned its citizens against making non-essential travel to Moyale town and its environs in light of the ongoing cross-border violence that has caused death, injuries and displaced thousands. ‎In an updated travel advisory issued on November 6, UK's Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) said the warning reflected its assessment of the deteriorating security situation and reports of cross-border incidents affecting the Kenyan side of the border with Ethiopia. ‎ advertisements The advisory covers Moyale town and an area extending five kilometres around it, including the border with Ethiopia. ‎"The travel advice update for Moyale town advises against all but essential travel. This reflects our assessment of the security situation and reports of cross-border incidents affecting the Kenyan side of the border," the FCDO said. ‎The warning comes as Kenyan security agencies step up operations along the border following fighting that erupted on October 22 in neighbouring Ethiopia. ‎Inspector General of Police Douglas Kanja on Thursday, November 5, ordered the deployment of additional officers to reinforce security in the border town. ‎During a security assessment visit, Kanja said officers had been directed to strengthen surveillance and remain on high alert to prevent the violence from spilling further into Kenya. ‎He also assured residents that the government was committed to protecting lives and property amid growing fears over stray ammunition. ‎ Kanja disclosed that two women, one Kenyan and another Ethiopian, had died after being struck by stray bullets, while several others had sustained injuries. ‎"One life has been lost on the Kenyan side after a woman was hit by a stray bullet on the neck. We have also recorded injuries arising from stray bullets. The best way to address this situation is to ensure the conflict is resolved quickly," he said. ‎The police chief also disclosed that approximately 10,000 displaced people were still living in temporary shelters and public institutions around Moyale, as humanitarian agencies continued providing emergency assistance. ‎The fighting has disrupted cross-border trade, movement of goods and services and electricity supply to Moyale, which relies heavily on power from Ethiopia. ‎The British advisory further maintains restrictions on several other parts of northern and eastern Kenya over terrorism threats, particularly from the Somalia-based al Shabaab militant group.‎ The FCDO advises against all travel to Mandera county, parts of Wajir county, most of Garissa county and parts of Lamu county. ‎It also advises against all but essential travel to Garissa Town, parts of Tana River county and sections of the coastline. ‎The latest warning adds to concerns over the security situation in the Horn of Africa, where instability across national borders continues to affect communities, trade and movement of people. ‎The FCDO said its travel advice is regularly reviewed as security conditions change, urging British nationals to consult its guidance before travelling. ‎The warning does not amount to a general travel ban on Kenya but specifically targets areas assessed to face heightened security risks. ethiopia.summary: The UK government has issued a travel advisory warning its citizens against non-essential travel to Moyale, Kenya, due to escalating violence linked to cross-border clashes with Ethiopia. The advisory, released on November 6 by the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), highlights the deteriorating security situation, including reports of incidents affecting the Kenyan side of the border. The advisory specifically targets Moyale and a five-kilometer radius around it. In response to the violence, which began on October 22, Kenyan authorities have intensified security measures, deploying additional officers to the area. Tragically, stray bullets have resulted in casualties, including the death of a woman in Kenya. Approximately 10,000 people have been displaced and are currently in temporary shelters. The FCDO's advisory also maintains travel restrictions in other parts of northern and eastern Kenya due to terrorism threats, particularly from the al Shabaab militant group. The situation reflects broader instability in the Horn of Africa.

ethiopia.summary: The U.S. has reaffirmed its commitment to Ethiopia's stability and security in the Horn of Africa during a meeting between U.S. Ambassador Ervin Massinga and Ethiopian Defense Minister Mohamed Idris. The discussions, held in Nairobi, focused on addressing regional security threats and promoting domestic peace initiatives. He reiterated the U.S. intention to maintain robust diplomatic and defense engagement to support peace efforts, counter regional instability, and encourage sustainable development throughout East Africa. This commitment underscores the U.S. role in enhancing security and stability in a region facing various challenges.

Twenty-one of the victims were civilians, while the remaining were members of the region’s anti-riot and militia forces. BBC Amharic cited the region’s police commission reporting that the incident took place Thursday in Daleti kebele, Buldiglo district of the Assossa zone. Endris Mohammed, the regional police commissioner, stated the attack occurred around 5 a.m. local time. He linked the attack to the militant group designated as a terrorist organization by the Ethiopian government, the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), commonly referred to by the government as “Shene”. Daleti Kebele shares a regional boundary with the Oromia region of Ethiopia. The militant group, believed to have clandestine support within government structures, has launched similar attacks across Oromia and neighboring border areas over the past seven years. Armed attacks by the group have previously targeted areas including Gurage, Somali, Sidama, and parts of the Benishangul-Gumuz region. According to the regional police commissioner, the assault in Daleti was a surprise attack, and the assailants fled the area shortly after. The Ethiopian Defense Force and regional security forces deployed to the area following the incident, restoring calm, according to the commissioner’s interview with BBC Amharic. The OLA has not commented on the attack at the time of writing. The group has been linked to recurring killings and kidnappings in the Oromia region. On Thursday, at least 38 Orthodox Christians were massacred in the Robe district of East Arsi, an attack regional authorities also linked to the OLA. The group also has a history of launching attacks in parts of the Amhara region, particularly around Ataye. The group has been making claims of “ military gain ” since March of this year. The attack temporarily displaced residents of Daleti and the surrounding district. Commissioner Endris told BBC Amharic that local officials held discussions with residents after the incident, and community members have since returned to their homes. __ Join our Telegram Channel : t.me/borkena Like borkena on Facebook Join the conversation. ethiopia.summary: In a tragic incident on Thursday morning, over 52 individuals were killed in the Buldiglo district of Ethiopia's Benishangul-Gumuz region. Among the victims, 21 were civilians, while the rest were local security forces. The attack occurred in Daleti kebele around 5 a.m. and has been attributed to the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), a militant group designated as a terrorist organization by the Ethiopian government. Regional police commissioner Endris Mohammed reported that the assailants fled the scene shortly after the attack. This incident is part of a troubling pattern of violence linked to the OLA, which has been responsible for similar attacks across various regions, including Oromia and Amhara. Following the assault, the Ethiopian Defense Force and regional security forces were deployed to restore order, and discussions with local residents were held to facilitate their return home. The OLA has not yet commented on this latest attack.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Through Al-Burhan’s Lens: The Making of a Neighbor Turned Adversary - horn review
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Through Al-Burhan’s Lens: The Making of a Neighbor Turned Adversary – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-11-07 Ethiopia Through Al-Burhan’s Lens: The Making of a Neighbor Turned Adversary 0 Comments One of the defining characteristics of leadership in the Horn of Africa is the extent to which the personal experiences, perceptions and characters of individual leaders shape how their countries behave and conduct their affairs. Eritrea, for instance, offers a clear example of how the state’s behavior has been shaped by Isaias Afwerki’s personal character and worldview. A similar dimension can be observed in Sudan. When Abdel Fattah al-Burhan became Chairman of Sudan’s Transitional Sovereignty Council in April 2019, effectively assuming the role of de facto head of state during the country’s delicate civil-military transition, his personal experiences, perceptions and political calculations became an important part of how Sudan and later the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), approached domestic and regional affairs. SAF’s leader Burhan’s approach towards Ethiopia is particularly revealing. Although Sudanese-Ethiopian relations have long been influenced by unresolved territorial questions, Nile politics and competing regional interests, the confrontation over Al-Fashaga from late 2020 acquired a distinctly personalized character. Burhan’s military background, his reported experience in the disputed territory during the 1990s and his pursuit of political legitimacy through a nationalist narrative of territorial takeover help explain the aggressiveness that characterized Sudan’s policy at the time and SAF’s position currently. These personal considerations did not operate independently of Sudan’s institutional interests or wider regional calculations. They reinforced one another, turning a longstanding border disagreement into a more consequential source of bilateral hostility. Burhan’s military career placed him close to Sudan’s border and security affairs long before he became the country’s most powerful political figure. He served in the border guards, later became their commander and held several senior military positions, including commander of the Ground Forces. He also worked as a trainer at a military college in eastern Sudan and served as Sudan’s military attaché in China. His professional experience included military training in Egypt and Jordan. This background is relevant when considering the strategic perspectives that may have informed his understanding of Ethiopia, particularly given Egypt’s longstanding tendency to view its eastern neighborhood through the lens of Nile security, territorial considerations and historical distrust. A particularly important time concerns his deployment to Al-Fashaga in 1995–96. Burhan served in the area during a period of considerable strain in Sudanese-Ethiopian relations following the 1995 assassination attempt against Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Addis Ababa. Ethiopia and Egypt accused Khartoum of involvement in the plot, while Sudan was already confronting territorial pressure elsewhere, including Egypt’s occupation of the Hala’ib and Shalateen area. Sudan’s government under Omar al-Bashir, preoccupied with the war against the Sudan People’s Liberation Army, did not mount a military response to the loss of territory. Burhan then reportedly felt humiliated by Sudan’s inability to defend ‘its territorial claims’. Nevertheless, it offers a possible explanation for why the takeover of Al-Fashaga later became so closely associated with his leadership. In 2020 when Ethiopia was consumed by the northern Ethiopia conflict, it opened an opportunity for the Chairman of the Transitional Sovereignty Council of Sudan, al-Burhan. He moved his forces into Al-Fashaga, displacing Ethiopian farmers and taking control of areas that had been cultivated by Ethiopians. The way the operation unfolded suggested that the deployment had been planned well in advance, as its speed and coordination made it unlikely to have been improvised. It has been also noted that Sudan deployed thousands of troops and that Burhan visited Gedaref shortly after the operation began, publicly declaring the armed forces’ determination to take the territory. Burhan’s personal involvement gave the operation a political significance beyond the border itself. Burhan’s personal role in driving the confrontation in Al-Fashaga has become so pronounced that some Sudanese officials and observers have come to characterize it as “Burhan’s war on Ethiopia.” His visits to the area, public statements and insistence that Sudan would take the territory helped frame the operation in a nationalistic tone. In March 2021, Burhan rejected negotiations that did not begin with Ethiopian recognition of Sudanese sovereignty over the disputed territory. The position left little room for the kind of pragmatic accommodation that had sustained the previous arrangement. The domestic political context was equally important in this matter. Sudan was experiencing a fragile transition in which the military leadership was competing with civilian actors over the direction and authority of the state. The border confrontation offered Burhan an opportunity to strengthen his nationalist credentials, consolidate support within the armed forces and present himself as a ‘defender of Sudanese territory’. Some senior military officers reportedly have commercial interests in Al-Fashaga, whose fertile agricultural land offered significant economic returns. These interests formed part of a wider pattern of military involvement in Sudan’s economy. There are hundreds of entities controlled by Sudanese security elites, spanning agriculture, banking and medical imports, illustrating the military establishment’s extensive economic reach. Sudan’s military establishment has long shared important characteristics with its Egyptian counterpart, particularly in its extensive commercial involvement across sectors extending well beyond the defense industry. The confrontation also developed within a wider regional alignment. Egypt and Sudan had intensified military cooperation through exercises after the ouster of Omar al-Bashir and signed a military cooperation agreement on March 2021. These developments coincided with tensions over the GERD and the failure of negotiations over the Nile. For Cairo, closer military coordination with Khartoum served its interest in strengthening a common position on the dam and also its own interests in Sudan. For Sudan’s military leadership, cooperation with Egypt provided diplomatic and military support at a moment when relations with Ethiopia were deteriorating. The implications of the above factors have extended beyond Al-Fashaga. During the same period, Sudan’s request for the removal of Ethiopian peacekeepers from the UN Interim Security Force for Abyei added another point of tension. On top of that, SAF also began leveraging cross-border proxies specifically targeting disgruntled ethnic groups in Ethiopia’s Benishangul-Gumuz region (BPLM and Gumuz dissidents). These dissident fighters frequently utilized the Sudanese borderlands (such as the Blue Nile region) as a logistical base and safe haven to launch incursions into western Ethiopia. This sort of position escalated after the outbreak of the Sudanese civil war between the SAF and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in 2023. The longstanding relation between veteran Tigrayan generals and Sudanese army has played a role for the subsequent Army 70’s (TPLF’s paramilitary group) direct participation on the side of al-Burhan. This resembles to the historical use of eastern Sudan as a supply route during the TPLF’s insurgency against the Derg. The conflict weakened Sudan’s ability to manage its border and increased the importance of external support for Burhan’s military campaign. Ethiopia, meanwhile, faced the prospect of instability spreading across its western border. In order to ease tension, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed travelled to Port Sudan and met Burhan in 2024, becoming the first foreign head of government to visit the Sudanese military leadership’s wartime capital. The visit was intended to encourage stability and explore possible paths towards peace. It demonstrated that Addis Ababa was still prepared to engage Burhan despite the tensions inherited from the Al-Fashaga confrontation. Yet the meeting did not produce a durable diplomatic breakthrough, and the two countries’ competing security concerns continued to deepen. As relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea deteriorated after Pretoria agreement, Asmara increasingly cultivated ties with armed opposition groups inside Ethiopia. These relationships would later intersect with Eritrea’s growing ties with Burhan, Burhan’s own relationship with the TPLF, and the connections both Eritrea and Sudan’s military leadership maintained with TPLF and other armed groups operating inside Ethiopia. What initially developed as separate relationships gradually converged, creating an overlapping network of political and military connections with direct implications for Ethiopia’s regional security. One of the clearest manifestations of this convergence came in mid-May 2026, when Port Sudan hosted a gathering under Tsimdo initiative, bringing together Ethiopian opposition figures and representatives associated with Eritrea and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF). The Port Sudan gatherings preceded by several months the establishment of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival in late September, followed by armed clashes between the groups and federal forces in northern Ethiopia. This has clearly shown that Sudan’s internal conflict had become increasingly intertwined with regional rivalries. Egypt openly strengthened its support for Burhan, while Eritrea developed closer relations with the SAF and hosted Sudanese military and political figures. These positions reflected shared interests over the regional balance of power, their respective strategic calculations and Egypt’s policies towards Ethiopia and Sudan. The historical pattern of Sudan’s military establishment aligning its Nile policy with Egyptian priorities has a long precedent. In November 1959, General Abboud’s military government signed the Nile Waters Agreement, conceding Egypt the larger share of the river’s water. Recently, the SAF-led authorities have again aligned Sudan’s Nile position with Cairo, reaffirming the 1959 Agreement , opposing Ethiopia’s operation of the GERD and pledging to protect Egypt’s water rights. The pattern suggests that, under Burhan, Sudan’s military leadership is once again being shaped by Egyptian priorities, even where these may not fully correspond with Sudan’s own long-term interests. Although Burhan and some senior military figures have adopted an increasingly confrontational posture towards Ethiopia, there are also influential figures within Sudan’s military-led establishment who recognize the costs of allowing tensions with Addis Ababa to develop into another front in an already devastating war. Malik Agar, deputy chairman of Sudan’s de facto Sovereign Council, has emerged as one of the clearest advocates of restraint . His behind-the-scenes efforts to ease tensions, including facilitating direct communication between Burhan and Abiy Ahmed during the May 2026 escalation, indicate an alternative approach within the Sudanese leadership. His subsequent public declaration that Sudan did not want a war with Ethiopia reinforced this position. Agar’s calculations are also shaped by the strategic realities of the Blue Nile region, where further confrontation with Ethiopia could create additional security pressures for Sudan. Figures such as Gibril Ibrahim, leader of the Justice and Equality Movement (JEM) and Sudan’s de facto finance minister, alongside General Ahmed Ibrahim Mufaddal, head of the General Intelligence Service (GIS) also participated in efforts to ease tensions. These diplomatic initiatives, however, have done little to temper the army’s increasingly confrontational public rhetoric. In essence, the SAF has continued to climb the escalation ladder, taking the deterioration of diplomatic relations to a new peak when it accused Ethiopia before the UN Security Council of supporting the RSF and facilitating its military operations from Ethiopian territory. Coming on the heels of the closure of consulates and the withdrawal of diplomatic personnel, the accusation represents another significant step in an increasingly rapid sequence of escalatory developments. That being said, the institutional interests of the SAF, the military’s economic position, the struggle for political authority in Sudan, the war against the RSF and the regional alignments surrounding the Nile and Red Sea have all contributed to the current situation. Burhan’s personal outlook appears to have intersected with these wider calculations, giving an unresolved border dispute a more persistent place in Sudan’s security policy. What began as a confrontation over territory has developed into a much broader strategic rivalry, one in which the stability of Ethiopia and Sudan is increasingly connected to the outcome of each other’s internal conflicts. ethiopia.summary: The article explores the evolving relationship between Sudan and Ethiopia through the lens of Sudanese military leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan. Since assuming leadership in 2019, Burhan's personal experiences and military background have significantly influenced Sudan's approach to Ethiopia, particularly regarding the disputed Al-Fashaga territory. The confrontation over this area intensified following Ethiopia's internal conflict in 2020, allowing Sudan to assert control and displace Ethiopian farmers. Burhan's actions have been framed as a nationalist endeavor, bolstering his political legitimacy amid Sudan's fragile civil-military transition. The article also highlights the broader regional dynamics, including Sudan's military cooperation with Egypt and the implications of the ongoing Sudanese civil war, which have intertwined with Ethiopia's security concerns. Despite attempts at diplomatic engagement, the relationship remains strained, with both nations navigating complex territorial and political challenges that threaten regional stability. The convergence of military and political interests complicates the path toward peace. (160 words)
