ethiopia.content: Ethiopia and Yemen: A Strategic Relationship Beyond Political Change – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-11-07 Ethiopia and Yemen: A Strategic Relationship Beyond Political Change 0 Comments For much of the past century, Ethiopia and Yemen have maintained a relationship shaped by geographical proximity, commercial interests and the changing political landscape of the Red Sea. Their relations have endured the collapse of monarchies, revolutionary governments, ideological confrontations and shifting regional alliances. Yet these political transformations have never diminished the strategic significance of the waters separating them. As competition over the Red Sea intensifies and maritime security becomes increasingly central to regional economic stability, Ethiopia has compelling reasons to reassess its engagement with Yemen. The challenge is no longer simply to preserve an established diplomatic relationship, but to translate historical connections into a more consequential foreign policy partnership. This requires sustained attention to developments across the Yemeni coastline, recognition of the interests both countries hold in each other’s stability, and a diplomatic approach capable of adapting to changing circumstances. The foundations of modern diplomatic relations date to March 1935, when Emperor Haile Selassie and Imam Yahya concluded a Treaty of Friendship and Commerce . The agreement formalized connections already sustained through generations of commercial exchange and migration. Yemeni merchant communities had established themselves in Ethiopian urban centers, contributing to trade and creating social relationships that extended beyond government diplomacy. These connections survived successive political transformations, demonstrating that relations between the two countries have often rested on interests more durable than the political circumstances of any particular period. Their significance lies in the continuity of engagement rather than the political arrangements through which that engagement occurred. The Cold War further demonstrated the adaptability of this relationship. South Yemen initially supported Eritrean liberation movements before reconsidering its regional position as Ethiopia’s Derg government strengthened relations with the Soviet Union. During the 1977 to 1978 Ogaden War, South Yemen supported Ethiopia against Somalia, and the two governments subsequently developed closer political and military cooperation. Their rapprochement culminated in a Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation in December 1979 . The realignment illustrated the limits of ideological commitments when confronted with changing security interests. Political differences did not disappear, but strategic calculations increasingly determined the direction of relations. The experience established an important precedent for Ethiopian diplomacy: regional interests can accommodate changes in political orientation when governments recognize the practical value of cooperation. Following Yemen’s unification in 1990 and Eritrea’s secession in 1993, Ethiopia’s maritime position changed fundamentally. Without direct sovereign access to the Red Sea, Ethiopia became increasingly dependent on neighboring maritime corridors and the political stability of the surrounding region. Relations with Yemen continued through an economic, scientific, technical and trade cooperation agreement signed in April 1999 and a security cooperation agreement concluded that October. These arrangements reflected an effort to preserve institutional cooperation despite the changing regional order. Yemen’s subsequent internal fragmentation, however, introduced complications requiring a more deliberate and flexible Ethiopian diplomatic approach. The historical relationship remains relevant, but its contemporary importance derives increasingly from Ethiopia’s economic dependence on maritime security and the political conditions prevailing across the Arabian shore. Yemen occupies one of the most consequential geographical positions in the Red Sea system. Its coastline borders maritime routes connecting the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean through Bab al Mandab and the Suez Canal. Political and security developments along this coast can influence commercial navigation, shipping insurance, international trade and regional stability. The International Maritime Organization has repeatedly warned that attacks against commercial vessels threaten the security of shipping and the stability of international supply chains. For Ethiopia, whose external commerce depends heavily on Djibouti, instability affecting these routes is not a distant maritime concern. It can increase transportation costs, disrupt supply chains and weaken the competitiveness of an economy seeking industrial expansion and stronger international market access. Although Ethiopia does not possess a Red Sea coastline, its economic future remains closely connected to the security of the surrounding maritime environment. This reality gives Ethiopia a compelling interest in maintaining an informed and active diplomatic presence in relation to Yemen. The country’s political landscape has produced competing centers of authority, while territorial administration remains an important factor in its maritime position. Ethiopia’s foreign policy must therefore recognize both the formal structures of diplomatic representation and the practical realities determining conditions along Yemen’s coastline. Addis Ababa would benefit from maintaining constructive channels of communication capable of responding to these realities without becoming entangled in Yemen’s domestic political competition. Such an approach would reflect Ethiopia’s longstanding tradition of diplomatic engagement across different political systems and changing regional alignments. Rather than allowing bilateral relations to depend exclusively on particular political circumstances, Ethiopia should cultivate lasting partnerships grounded in common economic, humanitarian and maritime interests. This approach would not require Ethiopia to abandon its established diplomatic principles or endorse the political positions of particular authorities. It would instead reflect the recognition that geographical interests endure even when political circumstances change. Ethiopia’s historical experience demonstrates that productive relations can develop across substantial ideological differences when both sides identify common priorities. Contemporary diplomacy should therefore emphasize continuity, discretion and practical cooperation, while remaining consistent with international obligations and the broader objective of regional stability. Such engagement would strengthen Ethiopia’s diplomatic presence and create opportunities for both countries to advance their long term strategic interests. The importance of this engagement becomes clearer when considered alongside Ethiopia’s wider maritime ambitions. Djibouti remains its principal commercial gateway, with World Bank assessments identifying the Djibouti corridor as the route carrying approximately 95 percent of Ethiopian trade at the time of the assessment. Somaliland’s Berbera port and Kenya’s Lamu corridor offer additional opportunities for diversification. These alternatives could reduce the economic risks associated with excessive dependence on one route, but infrastructure expansion alone cannot eliminate Ethiopia’s exposure to instability in the wider Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. Maritime security depends on political conditions extending beyond the territories through which Ethiopian cargo passes. Ethiopia must consequently complement port diversification with a diplomatic strategy that gives sustained attention to developments along Yemen’s maritime approaches. Expanding access to ports and strengthening the security of the routes serving them should be understood as complementary elements of the same national economic strategy. Yemen possesses equally important reasons to cultivate stronger relations with Ethiopia. Years of conflict have weakened its commercial institutions, damaged infrastructure and disrupted established trading networks. Ethiopia represents a substantial neighboring market and a potential partner in agricultural commerce, livestock trade, manufactured goods, logistics and associated services. In the longer term, improved economic connections with the African shore could support Yemen’s recovery and reduce its dependence on a narrow range of regional relationships. Ethiopia, meanwhile, could benefit from renewed commercial links extending through Yemen toward the Arabian Peninsula. These opportunities would require greater political stability, reliable institutions and improvements in transport infrastructure, but they provide a foundation for cooperation that reaches beyond immediate security concerns. The economic relationship could also acquire greater strategic importance as Ethiopia pursues industrial development and regional commercial integration. Reliable maritime access is essential not only for importing goods but also for expanding exports and attracting investment into manufacturing and logistics. Yemen’s eventual economic reconstruction could create opportunities for commercial cooperation and the restoration of trade networks historically connecting the two shores. Neither country would benefit from treating the other merely as a neighboring market. Their geographical proximity offers the possibility of a broader economic relationship in which transport, investment, commercial services and regional infrastructure reinforce one another. Realizing that potential would require gradual engagement and credible institutional commitments rather than ambitious agreements unsupported by prevailing conditions. Human mobility represents another significant dimension of their shared interests. Yemen has long served as a transit country for Ethiopian migrants traveling toward the Arabian Peninsula, exposing many to trafficking, exploitation and dangerous maritime crossings. According to the International Organization for Migration , approximately 506,600 outgoing movements were recorded along the wider Eastern Route in 2025, while an estimated 132,300 migrants were stranded in Yemen at the end of that year. These figures demonstrate that Yemen’s internal conditions have direct humanitarian consequences for Ethiopian citizens and place migration among the most important practical areas for diplomatic cooperation. The protection of migrants, humanitarian access and voluntary repatriation therefore deserve a more prominent position within Ethiopia’s relations with Yemen. The implications extend beyond humanitarian considerations. Irregular migration networks generate insecurity across transit corridors, expose vulnerable communities to organized criminal activity and place additional pressure on local institutions. For Ethiopia, the inability to protect citizens moving through Yemen can produce social and economic consequences at home. For Yemen, unregulated migration creates further difficulties for communities already affected by prolonged instability. Cooperation on migration would therefore serve both humanitarian and security interests. More consistent diplomatic consultation, coordination with international organizations and practical arrangements for protecting vulnerable migrants could provide measurable benefits even before broader political and economic cooperation becomes possible. These overlapping interests suggest that Ethiopia’s engagement with Yemen should be organized around a limited but carefully defined set of priorities. Maritime security should occupy a central position, particularly the protection of commercial navigation and the reduction of disruptions affecting Ethiopian trade. Economic diplomacy should seek to preserve existing commercial relationships while identifying realistic opportunities for future cooperation. Humanitarian engagement should prioritize migrant protection, voluntary returns and access to assistance. At the political level, Ethiopia should maintain sufficient diplomatic flexibility to communicate effectively as conditions evolve, while encouraging stability and avoiding unnecessary involvement in internal disputes. These priorities would provide greater continuity than a policy shaped primarily by reactions to individual crises. A more active policy would nevertheless require careful management of Ethiopia’s wider regional relationships. Yemen’s political circumstances are closely intertwined with the interests of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and other external actors, whose positions influence both its internal balance and the security environment of the Red Sea. Ethiopia maintains important economic and diplomatic relationships across the Gulf, making it essential that engagement with Yemen does not become associated with regional polarization. Addis Ababa should frame its approach around broadly shared interests in secure navigation, economic recovery, humanitarian protection and political stability. This would allow Ethiopia to advance its own objectives while preserving the diplomatic space necessary for cooperation with different regional partners. The more fundamental challenge is ensuring that Ethiopia’s policy becomes anticipatory rather than reactive. Maritime disruptions often draw diplomatic attention only after they produce measurable economic consequences, while political developments in neighboring regions may receive insufficient consideration until they affect established trade routes. Ethiopia’s dependence on the Red Sea demands a more sustained understanding of the political and security conditions affecting its maritime environment. Regular diplomatic assessments, institutional coordination and closer attention to changes along Yemen’s coastline would strengthen the country’s capacity to anticipate risks and identify opportunities. Such measures would not eliminate uncertainty, but they would reduce Ethiopia’s reliance on responses formulated after regional developments have already constrained its options. The history of Ethiopia and Yemen demonstrates that their relationship has repeatedly adapted to profound political transformations. From the diplomatic exchanges of the 1930s to the strategic realignments of the Cold War and the institutional cooperation of the 1990s, successive governments have found reasons to preserve relations despite differences in political orientation. Today, the stakes are considerably greater. Maritime security, economic diversification, migration and regional competition have made developments across the Red Sea increasingly consequential for both countries. Ethiopia should therefore approach Yemen as a permanent strategic consideration, investing in durable diplomatic relationships and practical cooperation that can withstand political uncertainty. The enduring value of the relationship lies not in any particular government or political arrangement, but in the recognition that the prosperity and security of both countries are closely connected to the stability of the maritime region they share. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia and Yemen have maintained a strategic relationship shaped by geographical proximity and shared interests for over a century, despite significant political changes. Their ties, formalized by a Treaty of Friendship and Commerce in 1935, have endured through various political upheavals, demonstrating that their relationship is rooted in mutual economic and maritime interests rather than solely political alignments. As Ethiopia lacks direct access to the Red Sea, it relies heavily on maritime security and regional stability for its economic growth, particularly through trade routes that pass through Yemen. Conversely, Yemen, weakened by years of conflict, sees Ethiopia as a vital market and partner for economic recovery. Both nations stand to benefit from enhanced cooperation in trade, infrastructure, and humanitarian efforts, particularly concerning migration issues. A diplomatic strategy that emphasizes continuity and practical cooperation can help both countries navigate their complex political landscapes while fostering long-term strategic interests.

somalia.title: A Partnership Under Strain: U.S. Reaffirms Support While Defunding the Mission Somalia Depends On - FTL Somalia
somalia.content: A Partnership Under Strain: U.S. Reaffirms Support While Defunding the Mission Somalia Depends On - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Security Nationwide A Partnership Under Strain: U.S. Reaffirms Support While Defunding the Mission Somalia Depends On November 8, 2026 6 min read MOGADISHU , Somalia’s Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi met with the U.S. Chargé d’Affaires, Ruth Anne Stevens-Klitz, on Sunday to discuss the future of the AUSSOM mission and the handover of a former AU base in Barawe to the Somali National Army, as Washington simultaneously reaffirms its security partnership and withdraws the funding that sustains the mission. According to a statement from the Ministry of Defence, the meeting focused on strengthening the strategic partnership between Somalia and the United States in defence and security, and on ongoing operations against the Khawaarij. The two sides specifically discussed the mandate and future of AUSSOM, emphasizing the importance of ensuring that the security transition is well-planned, coordinated, and based on the capabilities and readiness of the Somali National Armed Forces. The meeting also addressed the handover of a former AUSSOM military base in Barawe, which has now been taken over by the Somali National Army. The ministry described the handover as part of broader efforts to bolster the capacity of the national forces and to assume full responsibility for the country’s security. A Partnership Under Strain The Barawe handover is not an isolated event. It comes as Uganda withdraws its bilateral troops from the same region, and as AUSSOM prepares to take over positions that Ugandan forces are vacating. The Somali army commander, Brigadier General Ibrahim Mohamed Mohamud, visited Barawe last week to instruct troops to remain on high alert and intensify operations against Al-Shabaab , but the military statement did not clarify whether Somali forces would take over the AU bases being left behind. The broader context is one of a security architecture unravelling under financial pressure. The United States notified the African Union in July 2026 that it would end funding for the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS), which provides food, fuel, water, medical support, and casualty evacuation for AUSSOM’s roughly 12,000 personnel, as FTL Somalia reported on the U.S. decision to end UNSOS support . The UN support office has already begun preparing for liquidation, issuing a public tender to sell generators, medical equipment, and heavy machinery valued at approximately $30 million, as the unravelling security architecture has been documented. Washington has cited frustration with the Somali government’s failure to take full ownership of its security functions and sustain progress against Al-Shabaab. Yet the same U.S. officials who are withdrawing logistical support continue to engage with Somali security leadership on training and capacity-building. Stevens-Klitz’s meeting with Fiqi is a reaffirmation of a partnership that is simultaneously being defunded. As the Somali army chief’s earlier meeting with Stevens-Klitz demonstrated, military-to-military cooperation continues even as the financial foundations of the mission erode. The Barawe Handover and the Capability Question The handover of the Barawe base is a concrete step in the transition that AUSSOM’s mandate envisions. But it is also a test of whether the Somali National Army can hold territory that foreign forces have secured. Barawe was captured from Al-Shabaab in 2014, and the militants had used its port to bring in fighters and weapons and to export charcoal. Losing it would be a significant setback. As joint SNA and AUSSOM patrols in Barawe have shown, the transition from AU-led to Somali-led security in the region is already underway. The Somali forces taking over the base face the same constraints that have plagued the SNA across the country: limited logistics, payroll irregularities, and command-and-control weaknesses. Farhan Isak Yusuf, deputy executive director of Somali Public Agenda, warned that the Somali army lacks resources and faces a difficult security environment in Lower Shabelle, the region where the Ugandan troops were stationed and which is critical to protecting Mogadishu. Fiqi’s statement emphasized the government’s commitment to building a professional and capable national army, one fully equipped to fulfill its constitutional mandate. He expressed gratitude to the United States for its sustained support. But the gratitude is directed at a partner whose support is becoming more conditional and more limited, even as the security challenges mount. The return of the 22nd Gorgor Brigade from advanced training in Türkiye is a reminder that Somalia’s security partnerships extend beyond Washington, but the Gorgor brigades are a small elite force and cannot fill every gap left by departing AU troops. Critical Note The meeting between Fiqi and Stevens-Klitz takes place at a moment of profound contradiction in U.S.-Somalia security relations. Washington is simultaneously reaffirming its commitment to the Somali National Army and withdrawing the funding that sustains the AU mission the SNA depends on. The United States wants to help Somalia build its own forces while reducing its financial exposure to the broader security architecture. That is not an irrational policy. It reflects a legitimate frustration with the pace of progress and a reasonable expectation that Somalia should take increasing responsibility for its own security. But it is a policy that is being implemented in the middle of a political crisis, as the Supreme Court has declared the President’s mandate expired and the government’s authority is contested. The SNA is being asked to assume greater responsibility at the exact moment when the government that commands it is least able to provide the resources and direction it needs. The Barawe handover is a symbol of the transition. It is also a warning. A base handed over without the logistics to sustain it, without the payroll to pay the soldiers who hold it, and without the political consensus to legitimize the authority they represent is not a secure base. It is a position waiting to be tested. Al-Shabaab is preparing to exploit any vacuum left by departing foreign troops. The question is whether the Somali forces taking over Barawe are ready for that test, or whether the handover is a ceremony that precedes a retreat. somalia.summary: The U.S. reaffirmed its security partnership with Somalia during a meeting between Somali Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi and U.S. Chargé d’Affaires Ruth Anne Stevens-Klitz, despite simultaneously withdrawing funding for the AUSSOM mission, which is crucial for Somalia's security. The discussions included the handover of a former AU base in Barawe to the Somali National Army (SNA), highlighting the need for a well-coordinated security transition. However, this handover occurs amidst a backdrop of financial strain on the security architecture, as the U.S. has ceased funding for the UN Support Office in Somalia, which provides essential resources for AUSSOM personnel. The Somali army faces significant challenges, including limited logistics and command issues, raising concerns about its ability to maintain control over territories previously secured by foreign forces. The situation is further complicated by political instability, as the Somali government struggles to assert authority, leaving the SNA vulnerable to potential threats from Al-Shabaab.

somalia.content: Jowhar Celebrates Guudlaawe's Return While Hiiraan Mobilizes for Confrontation - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Politics Hirshabelle Jowhar Celebrates Guudlaawe’s Return While Hiiraan Mobilizes for Confrontation November 8, 2026 6 min read JOWHAR , Jowhar is hosting a stream of senior delegations from the Federal Government, regional administrations, and foreign missions on Sunday as the city prepares for the inauguration of re-elected Hirshabelle President Ali Abdullahi Hussein Guudlaawe, a ceremony that consolidates the ruling Justice and Solidarity Party’s control over yet another federal member state while the Hawadle community in Hiiraan remains in open revolt. South West State President Sheikh Adan Mohamed Nur Madobe arrived in Jowhar and was welcomed by Guudlaawe at Mohamed Dheere Airport, thanking him for attending the ceremony. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud is also expected in Jowhar, where he will inaugurate the reconstructed Jowhar Airport before attending the swearing-in, alongside other federal and regional officials and diplomats. The JSP Consolidation The inauguration follows Guudlaawe’s re-election on October 24, in which he secured 81 votes in the regional parliament, defeating Nur Ilmi Halane of the Ramaas party, as FTL Somalia reported on the parliamentary ballot . The Justice and Solidarity Party (JSP) holds 78 of the 99 seats in the regional assembly, giving Guudlaawe a commanding majority in a chamber that the ruling party dominates. This is the second federal member state inauguration in less than a week. As FTL Somalia reported on the Galmudug ceremony , Liibaan Ahmed Hassan was inaugurated in Dhusamareb on Thursday after the JSP secured a similar dominant majority in the Galmudug parliament. The pattern is now clear: Galmudug, Hirshabelle, and South West State are all under the effective control of the JSP and the federal government that backs it, while Puntland and Jubaland remain outside the fold and reject the federal electoral process entirely. The JSP’s regional strategy, backed by President Mohamud, has produced a string of victories in federal member state contests. As the September 30 direct elections demonstrated , the party won 158 of 222 local council seats and 78 of 99 House of the People seats in Hirshabelle, a landslide that set the stage for Guudlaawe’s return. But the parliamentary arithmetic that secured his re-election has not resolved the political dispute that has been building in Hiiraan since the JSP renominated him. The Hawadle Revolt The Hawadle community, dominant in Hiiraan, has rejected Guudlaawe’s re-election and the JSP’s power-sharing arrangement. As FTL Somalia reported when the dispute first escalated , Hawadle elders and politicians declared that any election held without a prior political agreement would be unacceptable, warning of unrest and holding the electoral committee responsible for the consequences. The dispute dates back to Hirshabelle’s formation in 2016, when an informal agreement allocated the presidency to the Hawadle, but the JSP’s renomination of Guudlaawe, an Abgaal from Middle Shabelle, deepened the grievance. The selection of Abdifatah Hassan Afrah, a former Hiiraan governor, as vice president was intended to balance the ticket, but it did not satisfy the Hawadle demand for the presidency itself. The situation escalated dramatically over the weekend. As FTL Somalia reported on the mobilization , Hawadle clan leader Ugaas Yusuf called for mass armed mobilization in Beledweyne, urging residents and security personnel from Hiiraan to prepare to defend the region against what he described as a planned federal government attack. Hundreds of residents reportedly mobilized with weapons, and there were unconfirmed reports that soldiers of Hawadle origin were defecting from the Somali National Army to join the standoff. Former Hirshabelle Parliament Speaker Osman Barre Mohamed backed the Ugaas and warned that a military offensive against Hiiraan would “lead to the collapse of the government itself.” Federal troops reportedly gathered at the Ugaas’s residence in Beledweyne on Saturday, and security personnel linked to NISA and local Macawisley militia remained in a standoff near the residence where Vice President Afrah was staying. The former NISA director, Abdullahi Mohamed Ali Sanbaloolshe, has returned to Beledweyne with an armed convoy and is positioning himself as the political leader of a movement seeking an independent administration for Hiiraan, as FTL Somalia reported on his arrival and the unravelling of Hirshabelle’s authority . Sanbaloolshe has backed calls for a separate Hiiraan administration and has not ruled out cooperation with Al-Shabaab . The mobilization also has implications for the fight against Al-Shabaab. The Macawisley fighters who have been drawn into the political dispute were among the most effective local forces in Hiiraan, and their withdrawal from the frontlines against the militants creates an opening that the group is likely to exploit. As FTL Somalia reported on the Hawadle-Al-Shabaab dynamic , the community’s sense of abandonment by the federal government has already pushed some of its leaders toward local agreements with the militants. Critical Note Guudlaawe’s inauguration is a victory for the JSP’s regional strategy. The party now controls Galmudug, Hirshabelle, and South West State, and it has done so with the federal government’s backing and the international community’s attendance. The parliamentary arithmetic is decisive, and the ceremony in Jowhar will project an image of normalcy and consolidation. But the image is misleading. A president elected by a chamber his party dominates, in a vote that the Hawadle leadership rejected as a sham, is not a president whose authority extends across the territory he claims to govern. As the outgoing Hawadle Vice President Yusuf Ahmed Hagar Dabageed said before the vote, “any result from that sham does not apply to Hiiraan.” The JSP has won the vote in Jowhar. It has not won the acceptance of Hiiraan. The armed mobilization in Beledweyne, the defections, and the standoff at the Vice President’s residence are not peripheral disturbances. They are the consequence of a political strategy that prioritized parliamentary control over consensus-building. The federal government’s role in this is central. President Mohamud backed Guudlaawe’s renomination, and the JSP’s dominance in regional assemblies is a product of federal influence as much as local popularity. The inauguration in Jowhar will be a celebration for the JSP and its allies. It will not be a resolution of the crisis in Hiiraan. The Hawadle leadership has chosen to mobilize rather than accept the outcome, and the federal government has chosen to back the JSP rather than mediate. The consequences of those choices will play out in Beledweyne, not in Jowhar, and they will not be resolved by a ceremony. somalia.content: Somalia opens first national pavilion at China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia opens first national pavilion at China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Saturday November 7, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somalia has opened its first national pavilion at the China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai on Thursday, showcasing agricultural products and investment opportunities as the government seeks to expand exports and strengthen trade relations with China. The pavilion was inaugurated by Somalia’s Minister of Commerce and Industry, Jama Mohamed Hassan, alongside Somalia’s Ambassador to China, Dr. Hodan Osman Abdi, during the ninth edition of the international trade exhibition. advertisements The ceremony was attended by senior Somali government officials, representatives of the Somali Chamber of Commerce and Industry, business leaders and members of the Somali delegation. Somali companies are displaying products including sesame seeds, frankincense and myrrh, while promoting investment opportunities in livestock, fisheries and mineral resources. The government hopes the exhibition will help Somali producers establish direct connections with Chinese importers, identify market requirements and secure new commercial partnerships. The expo, held at Shanghai’s National Exhibition and Convention Center from Nov. 5 to 10, has attracted 4,142 overseas exhibitors and participants from 162 countries, regions and international organizations, according to organizers. Somalia is among the countries participating in the expo’s national exhibition for the first time, providing a platform to introduce its products and investment potential to international buyers. The Somali Embassy in China said the initiative was intended to help domestic businesses understand Chinese market demands, improve product quality and develop commercial relationships that could lead to long-term export agreements. The exhibition also provides an opportunity to attract investment in local production, processing and packaging, which could enable Somali businesses to export more finished products rather than relying primarily on raw materials. “The Embassy of Somalia in China views this participation as a significant starting point for expanding the country’s exports and creating new markets that will benefit Somali farmers, livestock herders, fishers, and businesspeople,” the embassy said. The embassy credited the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, the Office of the Prime Minister, other government institutions and Somali entrepreneurs for coordinating the country's participation. It also praised Somali businesspeople based in China and those who traveled from Somalia for presenting products and investment opportunities at the pavilion. The embassy said it would continue facilitating connections between Somali and Chinese businesses and following up on commercial opportunities identified during the exhibition. Somalia’s participation comes as the government seeks to diversify export markets, attract foreign investment and strengthen the country's domestic production capacity. Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia Somalia: At Least Three Civilians Killed in Clashes Over Home Demolitions in Mogadishu Posted by: Horseed Staff At least three civilians were killed and several others seriously injured on Sunday during clashes between Somali security forces and residents protesting against the forced eviction and demolition of their homes in the capital, Mogadishu, according to former Prime Minister and presidential candidate Hassan Ali Khaire. 8 November, 2026 Share Tweet In a statement published on the social media platform X, Khaire said security forces opened fire on residents of the Warlaaliska neighborhood who had gathered to protest against forced evictions and what they described as the unlawful destruction of their properties. “Initial reports confirm, so far, three deaths and multiple serious injuries,” Khaire stated, holding the government fully responsible for the loss of life. He also called on the police to immediately halt the violence, protect civilians and end what he described as the suffering being inflicted on residents. According to local media reports, more than 200 homes were demolished during a coordinated operation launched early Sunday in Warlaaliska, located in Mogadishu’s Daynile district. #Video : Somalia police killed at least three protesters, including two youths during a demonstration against forced evictions in #Deynile district in #Mogadishu on Sunday, local media reported. They suggested that, several others sustained serious injuries too. #Somalia pic.twitter.com/oFDD56bE6n — Mohamed Omar✨️ (@Mhmd_Omar01) November 8, 2026 Residents allege that the land has been sold to a wealthy businessman with links to Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud. However, the allegations have not been independently verified. The demolitions reportedly took place despite previous government assurances that the neighborhood would not be affected. Those assurances followed an earlier confrontation in which residents opposed the deployment of security forces in the area. The incident has renewed concerns over forced evictions, property rights and the use of security forces in disputes over land ownership in Somalia. Somalia has faced decades of political instability and armed conflict since the overthrow of former President Mohamed Siad Barre in 1991. The collapse of the central government triggered years of civil war, the rise of rival armed factions and the emergence of Islamist militant groups, leaving the country struggling to restore stability and effective governance. somalia.title: The UN's exit from Somalia's political arena: What comes next? - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: The UN's exit from Somalia's political arena: What comes next? - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME OPINION The UN's exit from Somalia's political arena: What comes next? Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Hussein Shegow Mohamed Sunday November 8, 2026 After more than three decades, the United Nations political mission in Somalia closes today. The country asked for it. The harder question is whether its institutions are ready. The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) concludes its mandate on 31 October 2026. On October 31, 2026, the UN ends its political mission in Somalia. A ceremony was held in Mogadishu earlier that week to commemorate the conclusion of 13 years of work that began with the creation of UNSOM in 2013. If you go back a little further, the story is older. In 1995, a political office was established by the UN for Somalia. Thus, it is not the end of a single mission when the doors close. It's the end of a long-standing habit. People are already asking what happens now. It's a fair question, and I don't think the honest answer is either "everything will be fine" or "the country will fall apart." advertisements Let's begin with something that is frequently overlooked. This was requested by Somalia. The foreign minister requested in a letter to the Security Council in May 2024 that the mission's mandate expire in October of that same year. Later, Mogadishu consented to a more gradual departure, and the Council unanimously approved a two-year transition that would conclude on October 31, 2026, with the mission being renamed UNTMIS. Its responsibilities were supposed to be transferred to Somali institutions and the remaining UN agencies. And they do remain. After the mandate expires, the UN has stated that it will continue to support Somalia. Humanitarian organizations, development initiatives, clinic staff, and food distributors all continue to exist. The political office, which consisted of a small team of advisors and diplomats tasked with reaching out to all parties, negotiating agreements, and documenting issues, disappears. That final point, in my opinion, is more important than we realize. Anyone who has followed Somali politics is aware of how frequently the real struggle is not with Al-Shabaab but rather between Mogadishu and the federal member states over issues like elections, the constitution, and power. Someone had to sit in the middle and be trusted by both parties when those discussions broke down in the past. Although it wasn't flawless, the UN was typically trusted enough to bring people together. Now, who does that? The Union of Africa? adjacent governments? The Gulf states, Turkey? Everyone in the room is aware of their shared interests in Somalia. An exit works when local institutions are already strong enough to carry the load, and it hurts when the exit date arrives before they are. Lessons from Liberia Examining another nation that experienced a similar situation is beneficial. I keep thinking about Liberia as an example. After fifteen years, UNMIL, the UN peacekeeping force stationed there, came to an end in March 2018. Liberia had recently accomplished something that many had doubted it could: in 2017, a president peacefully transferred power to a successor through an election, something that hadn't happened in decades. The exit was hailed as evidence of the nation's maturity. And it had, in certain respects. However, the institutions that were meant to keep things together proved to be weaker than the festivities suggested as Liberia battled complaints of corruption, growing costs, and street demonstrations in the years that followed. It is crucial to note that the nation did not return to war. However, the blue helmets' departure did not end the quiet process of reestablishing trust. Here, I should exercise caution. The closure in Somalia is a political mission, and UNMIL was a peacekeeping force with soldiers and police; the two are not the same. Liberia did not have an ongoing insurgency in 2018, but Somalia does. The lesson is still applicable, though. Three things to watch So where does Somalia stand? I'd say there are three things worth watching. The first is the election. The entire transition will appear to be successful if the major players agree to move on to the next round. We will soon learn the practical consequences of the UN's absence if it results in a disagreement over the regulations. The second is rights to humanity. In order to document abuses and speak out, journalists, activists, and displaced families depended on the mission. The government claims that national organizations can take over, and perhaps they can, but only if they are granted autonomy. It is not much of a commission if it is unable to hold the funders accountable. Thirdly, there is security. Al-Shabaab has not disappeared, and the African Union has not yet completed the transfer of security responsibilities. Weakness in the military and political disputes feed each other. Every time leaders engage in combat, the rebels gain ground. A test of ownership This does not imply that the choice was incorrect. A nation cannot continue to be governed by foreign powers indefinitely, and many Somalis were fed up with the idea that foreign powers controlled their politics. It makes sense to want to control your own destiny. Owning it, however, entails doing the difficult part, which entails making concessions, putting up with regulations that occasionally work against you, and creating institutions that outlive any one president. The UN is no longer involved in politics. We won't know for a few years whether that was courageous or premature. We do know that if the negotiations fail, no one else will be held accountable going forward. __________________________ Hussein Shegow Mohamed is a Somali writer and political and security analyst. He holds a Master’s degree in International Relations and Diplomacy and a Bachelor’s degree in International Relations. His work focuses on Somalia’s security, governance, and sustainable peace. This decision was initiated by the Somali government, which requested the UN's exit in a letter to the Security Council in May 2024. The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) was established in 2013, but its roots trace back to a political office set up in 1995. As the UN departs, concerns arise about the readiness of Somali institutions to manage political disputes, particularly regarding elections and governance. The UN's absence raises questions about who will mediate conflicts between Mogadishu and federal member states, especially with ongoing threats from Al-Shabaab. somalia.title: Somalia’s Constitutional Test: Presidential power must answer to law - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Somalia’s Constitutional Test: Presidential power must answer to law - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME OPINION Somalia’s Constitutional Test: Presidential power must answer to law Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Hirsi Abdulkadir Mohamed Sunday November 8, 2026 A constitutional limit means little if a president can respond to judicial scrutiny by replacing the leadership of the court examining his authority. That is the principle at stake in Somalia’s confrontation between the presidency and the judiciary. On 7 November 2026, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud attended the swearing-in of Ibrahim Idle Suleiman as Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. He emphasized judicial independence, accountability and equal justice. Yet the circumstances surrounding the appointment raise a fundamental question: will the presidency accept those principles when they constrain its own power? Two days earlier, the Supreme Court reportedly ruled that the mandates of Somalia’s federal institutions had expired. It held that constitutional amendments increasing terms from four to five years did not automatically grant existing officeholders another year. The court directed political stakeholders to agree on an electoral framework within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, while limiting the government to routine administration. advertisements The dispute concerns more than the timing of an election. It tests whether Somalia’s constitutional institutions can impose meaningful limits on those who govern. Under Articles 60 and 91 of the 2012 Provisional Constitution, parliamentary and presidential terms were four years. Any claim to an additional year therefore depends on the legal effect of subsequent amendments, particularly their transitional provisions. Changing the length of future terms and extending an incumbent’s mandate are distinct legal acts. The latter requires a clear constitutional foundation because it changes the conditions under which authority was originally entrusted. Without that distinction, constitutional reform risks becoming a mechanism through which officeholders prolong their own rule. The ambition to introduce direct elections does not remove this obligation. Electoral reform must proceed through lawful institutions and procedures. Its democratic promise cannot, by itself, authorize an extension of power. The judicial leadership dispute makes the situation more serious. President Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed before the mandate ruling, citing concerns about the administration of justice. The Supreme Court subsequently declared the dismissal unconstitutional and accused the president of interfering with a pending constitutional case. The replacement’s swearing-in nevertheless proceeded. This sequence raises substantial concerns about executive interference, although timing alone does not establish personal motives. The presidency must explain the legal basis for removing the previous Chief Justice and appointing his successor while its own mandate is under judicial examination. Article 90(j) of the 2012 constitutional text connects presidential judicial appointments to recommendations from the Judicial Service Commission. Article 111A assigns that commission responsibilities concerning judicial recruitment and dismissal. The government should publish the relevant decrees and demonstrate compliance with the applicable framework, including any subsequent legal changes. A swearing-in ceremony cannot cure an appointment made without lawful authority. Nor does replacing a Chief Justice reverse an existing judgment. Any challenge to the court’s decision must follow an authorized legal process. The judiciary must also establish the basis of its authority. The 2012 constitutional framework assigns important constitutional functions to a distinct Constitutional Court. A complete assessment must therefore explain how the Supreme Court’s Constitutional Division acquired jurisdiction over this dispute, including through any applicable transitional legislation. The authenticated judgment, operative constitutional amendments and relevant judicial laws should be publicly accessible. Questions about jurisdiction or procedure deserve reasoned answers through lawful channels. They cannot simply become a justification for executive disregard. Meanwhile, Somalia must preserve essential public administration. Salaries, services and security responsibilities cannot be suspended while political leaders contest their mandates. But administrative continuity does not automatically preserve unrestricted presidential powers. If the reported caretaker limitations are legally effective, a consequential judicial appointment requires a specific legal justification. International partners should support transparency, judicial independence and an inclusive electoral settlement with clear deadlines. Their pursuit of stability must reinforce constitutional accountability. Accepting indefinite uncertainty over mandates would weaken the institutions on which lasting stability depends. Federal authorities, Federal Member States and opposition leaders must negotiate a credible electoral process while protecting peaceful political participation and the judiciary’s freedom to act. Political agreement can facilitate a lawful transition; it cannot permanently replace constitutional authority. President Mohamud has called for judicial independence. He should demonstrate that commitment by submitting his administration’s claimed mandate and judicial appointments to transparent legal scrutiny. The Constitution must bind the presidency when compliance carries a political cost. Otherwise, Somalia risks establishing a dangerous precedent: that those entrusted with power may decide for themselves when its limits apply. _________________________________ Hirsi Abdulkadir Mohamed is a lawyer and Horn of Africa political analyst. football.title: دفعة مزدوجة لمنتخب السودان قبل موقعة السنغال - winwin
football.content: دفعة مزدوجة لمنتخب السودان قبل موقعة السنغال دفعة مزدوجة لمنتخب السودان قبل موقعة السنغال مباريات اليوم رياضات كرة القدم الأخبار فيديو البطولات البرامج دول دفعة مزدوجة لمنتخب السودان قبل موقعة السنغال الغاني جيمس كواسي أبياه مدرب منتخب السودان (Facebook/ SFA) 6 نوفمبر 2026 دفعة مزدوجة لمنتخب السودان قبل موقعة السنغال السودان السنغال تصفيات كأس الأمم الأفريقية كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' كثف منتخب السودان استعداداته خلال معسكره القصير بالعاصمة كيغالي، تأهبًا لمواجهتي السنغال الحاسمتين، المقررتين يومي 12 و16 نوفمبر الجاري، ضمن الجولتين الثالثة والرابعة من المجموعة العاشرة في التصفيات المؤهلة لبطولة الأمم الأفريقية 2027 . وبدد طبيب المنتخب مخاوف الجماهير بعد تعرض حارس المرمى فريد مصطفى لعارض صحي طارئ استدعى نقله للمستشفى، فيما سيتلقى المدرب كواسي أبياه المزيد من الدعم بانضمام نجوم الهلال والمريخ للتدريبات. صفوف منتخب السودان تكتمل بانضمام نجوم العملاقين يلتحق نجوم الهلال والمريخ اليوم الجمعة 6 نوفمبر/ تشرين الثاني، بتدريبات "صقور الجديان" في العاصمة الرواندية كيغالي، بعد غيابهم عن الحصة التدريبية الأولى التي اقتصرت على المحترفين في الخارج واللاعبين الشباب الجدد في قائمة المدرب كواسي أبياه. ويسيطر نجوم العملاقين على قائمة مدرب السودان بوجود 19 لاعبًا يمثلون القوام الأساسي للمنتخب، في مشهد طبيعي لاستمرار الفريقين بالمنافسات المحلية والقارية، وكان المدرب قد منح الفرصة للاعبي الفريقين للمشاركة في مبارياتهما مؤخرًا بالدوري الرواندي، مفضلًا استمرارهم في التنافس الرسمي. اقرأ أيضًا بخطوة غريبة.. مدرب السودان يثير الجدل قبل مواجهتي السنغال مفاجآت وعائدون.. أبياه يكشف قائمة السودان لمواجهتي السنغال وفي سياق منفصل طمأن الطاقم الطبي الجماهير على الحالة الصحية لحارس المرمى الواعد فريد مصطفى، بعد أن تجاوز وعكة صحية طارئة استدعت نقله إلى المستشفى عقب الحصة التدريبية الأولى التي خاضها صقور الجديان. وأكد طبيب منتخب السودان محمد النعيم، في حديث للموقع الرسمي لاتحاد الكرة، سلامة اللاعب بناء على نتائج الفحوص، موضحًا أنه سيستأنف تدريباته مع زملائه بشكل طبيعي بعد حصوله على قسط قصير من الراحة. من جهة أخرى، سيخوض المنتخب السوداني 3 حصص تدريبية في ختام معسكره بكيغالي، قبل التوجه إلى داكار يوم 9 نوفمبر، استعدادًا لمواجهة السنغال يومي 12 و16 من الشهر ذاته، ضمن الجولتين الثالثة والرابعة من التصفيات الأفريقية؛ حيث يطمح المنتخب لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية تنعش حظوظه في بلوغ النهائيات. النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية لتصلك آخر أخبار الرياضة اشترك معنا دول كرة القدم الأخبار الدوريات الفرق رياضات التنس كرة السلة رياضات ميكانيكية football.summary: كثف منتخب السودان استعداداته لمواجهتي السنغال الحاسمتين، المقررتين في 12 و16 نوفمبر، ضمن تصفيات كأس الأمم الأفريقية 2027. يأتي ذلك بعد أن انضم نجوم الهلال والمريخ إلى التدريبات في كيغالي، بعد غيابهم عن الحصة التدريبية الأولى التي اقتصرت على المحترفين واللاعبين الشباب. يضم المنتخب 19 لاعبًا من الفريقين، مما يعكس قوة التشكيلة الأساسية. من جهة أخرى، طمأن الطاقم الطبي الجماهير بشأن حالة حارس المرمى فريد مصطفى، الذي تعرض لوعكة صحية استدعت نقله للمستشفى، حيث أكد الطبيب محمد النعيم أنه سيستأنف تدريباته بعد فترة راحة قصيرة. يهدف المنتخب السوداني لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية في المباراتين لتعزيز فرصه في التأهل للنهائيات. سيخوض الفريق ثلاث حصص تدريبية قبل مغادرته إلى داكار في 9 نوفمبر.
